Day 1
From Hotel: 9 min → World of Coca-Cola
1. World of Coca-Cola
The flagship museum of the drink invented in Atlanta, on a plaza named for the pharmacist who first mixed it. The vault holding the secret formula, a century of advertising art, and a tasting room pouring more than 100 Coca-Cola products from around the world make it a uniquely Atlanta visit.

3 min · 1 min → National Center for Civil and Human Rights
2. National Center for Civil and Human Rights
A powerful museum connecting the American civil rights movement to global human rights struggles. The lunch-counter sit-in simulation — headphones on, hands on the counter — is one of the most affecting museum experiences in the country, and the gallery of Dr. King's personal papers grounds it all in Atlanta.

3. Georgia Aquarium
One of the largest aquariums in the world — ten million gallons and the only whale sharks on display outside Asia. The Ocean Voyager tunnel sends you through a habitat where the giants glide overhead alongside manta rays, an experience no other aquarium in the Western Hemisphere offers.

Day 2
From Hotel: 5 min · 1 min → High Museum of Art
1. High Museum of Art
The leading art museum of the South, as famous for its architecture as its collection — Richard Meier's white-porcelain building won him the Pritzker Prize, and Renzo Piano later doubled it. Inside: American decorative arts, self-taught Southern artists, and a sunlit atrium ramp worth the visit alone.

15 min · 5 min → Piedmont Park
2. Piedmont Park
Atlanta's great lawn — 200 rolling acres laid out on the old Gentlemen's Driving Club grounds, where the Midtown skyline rises over Lake Clara Meer in the city's most photographed view. Joggers, picnics, and dog parks fill the meadows, and the Eastside BeltLine and Botanical Garden both touch its edges.

3. Atlanta Botanical Garden
Thirty acres on the edge of Piedmont Park, crowned by the glass Fuqua Conservatory and the Canopy Walk — a 600-foot skywalk through the treetops of an urban hardwood forest. The orchid house holds the largest collection in the country, and summer evenings bring sculpture and light installations to the paths.

Day 3
From Hotel: 8 min → Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park
1. Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park
The blocks of Sweet Auburn where Dr. King was born, preached, and now rests. Historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, the King Center with the crypt of Dr. and Mrs. King beside a reflecting pool, and the eternal flame sit within a few steps of each other. Start at the visitor center for the exhibits and the film.
Read more

27 min · 3 min → Historic Oakland Cemetery
2. Historic Oakland Cemetery
Founded in 1850, Oakland is a 48-acre Victorian garden cemetery — final resting place of six Georgia governors, Margaret Mitchell, and Bobby Jones. Ancient oaks, magnolias, and elaborate 19th-century funerary sculpture make it one of the most atmospheric open spaces in Atlanta.
Read more
Open 24/7
~1 hr 30 min

38 min · 5 min → Inman Park
3. Inman Park
Atlanta's first planned residential suburb, laid out in 1890 with curving boulevards, pocket parks, and Queen Anne and Craftsman mansions. The streetcar suburb fell into decay, was saved by early preservationists in the 1970s, and now anchors Atlanta's most walkable historic neighborhood.
Read more

4. Little Five Points
Atlanta's counterculture hub since the 1980s — built around the intersection of Moreland, Euclid, and McLendon avenues. Independent record stores, vintage clothing, tattoo parlors, and street murals with no major chains in sight.

5. Jimmy Carter Presidential Library and Museum
Opened in 1986, the museum preserves 27 million documents from Carter's presidency alongside a full-scale Oval Office replica and his Nobel Peace Prize medal. The 35-acre parklike campus — Japanese gardens, two small lakes, and Atlanta skyline views — sits off Freedom Parkway.

Day 4
From Hotel: 19 min · 3 min → Margaret Mitchell House
1. Margaret Mitchell House
The Tudor Revival apartment building on Peachtree where Mitchell lived from 1925 to 1932 and wrote Gone with the Wind, calling the cramped flat "The Dump." The house burned twice — 1994 and 1996 — and was restored. Guided tours run every 30 minutes through the apartment and a photo gallery.

29 min · 5 min → Virginia-Highland
2. Virginia-Highland
Atlanta's best-preserved streetcar suburb, laid out in 1912 along the Nine-Mile Circle streetcar line and named for the intersection of Virginia Avenue and North Highland Avenue at its center. The commercial strip concentrates independent bookstores, bars, and restaurants in storefronts unchanged since the 1930s.

9 min → Fernbank Museum of Natural History
3. Fernbank Museum of Natural History
Opened in 1992 on a 65-acre old-growth Piedmont forest campus in Druid Hills, Fernbank's signature exhibit — Giants of the Mesozoic — displays a 123-foot Argentinosaurus alongside a Giganotosaurus at full scale, the largest dinosaur pair on exhibit in the Eastern United States.

Local Tastes
Lemon Pepper Wings
Atlanta's signature chicken wing — dusted in lemon pepper, often finished wet with lemon-butter sauce. Born in the city's wing shops and now an emblem of Atlanta food culture, name-checked in hip-hop and television alike.
J.R. Crickets
The Frosted Orange
The creamy orange shake of The Varsity, the world's largest drive-in, slinging chili dogs and onion rings two blocks from the hotel for nearly a century. Order an F.O. with a chili dog and eat under the neon.
The Varsity
Fried Chicken & Pot Likker
The classic Atlanta meat-and-three plate — skillet fried chicken with collard greens and a cup of pot likker, the smoky broth left from the greens, served with cracklin' cornbread for dipping.
Mary Mac's Tea Room · The Busy Bee Café
Peach Cobbler
Georgia is the Peach State, and its cobbler — buttery crust over baked spiced peaches, usually under vanilla ice cream — is the dessert Atlanta's soul food kitchens are judged by.
Mary Mac's Tea Room · Paschal's
Food Delivery
DoorDash
Foreign number: not accepted. — the code arrives by SMS to a US number, and DoorDash serves only the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, so a foreign SIM has nowhere to receive it.
The longest restaurant list in Atlanta by some margin, and the one that still reaches out into the suburbs where the others thin out. Strong on late-night delivery around Midtown and the Old Fourth Ward — but it needs a US number to set up.
doordash.com
Uber Eats
Foreign number: accepted. — it runs on the same Uber account, so the code comes by SMS to any international number, with a voice call as the fallback.
The visitor's way in, since it runs on the Uber account you already have. A shorter list than DoorDash, but solid across Midtown, Downtown and the BeltLine corridor, and its delivery estimates hold up well in Atlanta traffic.
ubereats.com

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted. — the code comes by SMS to any international number, and "Call me with code" reads it out if the SMS is blocked.
Atlanta is spread out and MARTA rail reaches only a slice of it, so ride-hailing covers the gaps between Midtown, Buckhead, the BeltLine and Hartsfield-Jackson. Cars are plentiful; expect surge pricing around Braves and Falcons games.
uber.com
Lyft
Foreign number: not accepted. — Lyft's own help says the number must be a US, Canadian or Puerto Rican one, and the code is texted only to that number.
Runs alongside Uber across the metro with much the same coverage, and fares often undercut it outside peak hours, so it is worth having both open to compare. Registration is the catch, and it is a hard one for a visitor.
lyft.com

MLK Birth Home — Closed for Rehabilitation
The Birth Home at 501 Auburn Ave is closed for a major rehabilitation project — no interior tours.
Fox Theatre — Tours three days a week
Guided tours run Monday, Thursday and Saturday only; the auditorium is otherwise open just on show nights.

Worth Knowing

Peachtree Notes

The hotel and the Fox Theatre have been staring at each other across Peachtree Street for nearly a century. When Gone with the Wind premiered in Atlanta, the stars screened the film down the street and the celebration gala filled the hotel's ballrooms — while the Fox's own survival later came down to a grassroots campaign of schoolchildren's pennies and benefit concerts that saved it from becoming a parking lot.

Day 1 traces a quieter thread: the Coca-Cola fortune that built Pemberton Place also helped fund the city's civil rights institutions, and Atlanta's old nickname — the city too busy to hate — was coined by the same business establishment whose skyline now forms the backdrop to Dr. King's crypt on Auburn Avenue. Commerce and conscience have always shared this city's streets.
